summary: Describes a simple, fully specified Forward Error Correction scheme using Reed-Solomon codes over Galois fields, for protecting media streams in the FECFRAME framework. These codes give optimal protection against packet loss: with enough repair packets, lost data can be rebuilt.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a few extra puzzle pieces along with the real ones, so if some get lost the receiver can still finish the picture.

questions: how to recover lost packets in media streams
how does fecframe recover lost packets
subtitle: A Reed-Solomon recipe for rebuilding lost packets in media streams, with optimal recovery and a simple packet layout.

tldr.problem: Media streams lose packets, and the FECFRAME framework needs a concrete FEC scheme that recovers as much as possible from the repair data it sends.
tldr.mechanism: Each application data unit becomes one source symbol, padded to a common length with a 3-byte prefix, and Reed-Solomon coding over GF(2^m) produces repair symbols, one per repair packet, tagged with a small payload ID.
tldr.outcome: Any k encoding symbols are enough to recover the k source symbols, at the price of limits on block size and higher computation than LDPC codes. The scheme is registered as FEC Encoding ID 8.

facts.label: ADU prefix
facts.value: 3 bytes (1 byte flow ID, 2 bytes length)

today: RFC 6865 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata. It registers FEC Encoding ID 8 in the FECFRAME FEC Encoding IDs subregistry.

sections.title: Why Reed-Solomon for FECFRAME
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) improves the reliability of unicast, multicast and broadcast delivery by sending extra data that lets receivers repair losses. RFC 6363 defines a generic framework (FECFRAME) for using FEC schemes with media delivery applications, for instance real-time streaming over RTP. This document supplies one fully specified scheme for it.

The Reed-Solomon codes used here are Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) codes, which are optimal for recovering erasures: a receiver can recover the k source symbols from any set of exactly k encoding symbols. They are also systematic, meaning the source symbols are themselves part of the encoding symbols. The drawbacks are a limit on the maximum source block size and number of encoding symbols, and a higher encoding and decoding cost than the sparse-matrix codes of RFC 5053 or RFC 5170.

The scheme is meant to be compatible with the widely used Reed-Solomon codec of Luigi Rizzo. It inherits the core code definitions (Vandermonde-matrix based) from Section 8 of RFC 5510 and replaces the formats and procedures meant for the RFC 5052 framework with FECFRAME-specific ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra pieces here are very clever: with enough of them, you can always rebuild what is missing. The catch is that the puzzle cannot be too big, and working out the spare pieces takes some effort.

sections.title: Symbols, Blocks and Notation
sections.content:
An Application Data Unit (ADU) is the unit of source data handed to the transport layer, such as an RTP packet. A group of ADUs treated together is an ADU block. In this scheme there is always one source symbol per ADU, and one source block per ADU block. A repair symbol is an encoding symbol that is not a source symbol, and the code rate is k/n, the number of source symbols over the number of encoding symbols.

The notation used throughout: k is the number of source symbols in a block, n the number of encoding symbols, E the encoding symbol length in bytes, m the length of finite field elements in bits (with 2 <= m <= 16), and q = 2^m the number of field elements. B is the number of ADUs in a block and max_B its maximum.

Three restrictions are stated with MUST: exactly one source symbol per ADU Information unit, exactly one repair symbol per FEC repair packet, and exactly one source block per ADU block.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of each message as one card. Cards are gathered into a pile, and for each pile the sender makes some extra backup cards. One backup card travels in each envelope.

sections.title: Sizing ADU Blocks
sections.content:
Two limits cap how many ADUs can go in one block. The finite field size m caps the number of encoding symbols at 2^m - 1; with the default m = 8 that is 255, so k < n <= 255. Given the target code rate CR, the sender computes max_k = floor((2^m - 1) * CR), which leaves room for the desired number of repair symbols.

Real-time needs set the second limit. A larger block means a decoder may wait longer to collect enough symbols, so decoding delay grows with block size. With a maximum decoding latency l and each ADU covering duration d of constant bit-rate media, the block must not exceed max_rt = floor(l / d). The RFC's example is d = 10 ms and l = 1 s, giving max_rt = 100 ADUs. The final bound is max_B = min(max_k, max_rt).
sections.plainLanguage: A pile of cards cannot be too tall. The code only allows so many cards, and waiting for a very tall pile to fill makes the show lag.

sections.title: Building the Source Block
sections.content:
Reed-Solomon coding needs every symbol in a block to be the same length E, but ADUs vary in size (frames in an H.264 Group of Pictures, for example). So each ADU is wrapped into an ADU Information (ADUI) unit before encoding. Three bytes are prepended: F[i], one byte naming the ADU flow (so no more than 256 flows per FECFRAME instance), and L[i], two bytes giving the ADU length in network byte order. Zero padding Pad[i] then fills the unit to exactly E bytes.

When E is set per block (flag S = 0, the default), it equals the largest ADU in the block plus 3, and a receiver learns it from the first repair packet it gets. When E is fixed (S = 1), it must be at least the largest ADU plus 3, otherwise an error is returned and handling it is left to the use case.

The 3 prefix bytes and the padding are never sent. They are still part of the encoding, so a receiver that rebuilds a lost ADUI can strip the padding and identify the flow.
sections.plainLanguage: To make all the cards the same size, short ones get blank space added, and a tiny label says which stream each belongs to and how long it really is. The blank space and label are not mailed; they are worked out again at the other end.

sections.title: Configuration and Payload IDs
sections.content:
The FEC Framework Configuration Information (FFCI) must reach both sides. Its mandatory part is the FEC Encoding ID, which MUST be 8. The scheme-specific part (FSSI) holds E (an integer below 2^16), the Strict flag S, and m. With SDP, it is carried in the fec-repair-flow attribute, for example a=fec-repair-flow: encoding-id=8; fssi=E:1400,S:0,m:8. As an opaque string, the FSSI is 3 octets: a 16-bit E, a 1-bit S and a 7-bit m.

A FEC source packet carries its ADU followed by an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID. A FEC repair packet carries a Repair FEC Payload ID before its single repair symbol. Both IDs hold a Source Block Number (SBN, 32-m bits), an Encoding Symbol ID (ESI, m bits) and a 16-bit Source Block Length k. For source symbols 0 <= ESI <= k - 1; for repair symbols k <= ESI <= n - 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Each envelope gets a small label: which pile it belongs to, which card number it is, and how many cards the pile has. The label is the same size and shape for every envelope.

sections.title: Sender Procedures
sections.content:
Block creation follows the ADUI rules above. The SBN MUST start at 0 for the first block of the ADU flow and MUST increase by 1 for each new source block. For long sessions it wraps to zero after 2^(32-m) - 1. The ESI MUST start at 0 and be managed sequentially, so the first k values identify source symbols and the last n-k values identify repair symbols.

The core code itself is not redefined here. The document inherits the Reed-Solomon codes based on Vandermonde matrices from Section 8 of RFC 5510.
sections.plainLanguage: Piles and cards are simply numbered in order, starting from zero. The first cards in each pile are the real ones; the ones after them are backups.

sections.title: Choosing the Field Size
sections.content:
The default m = 8 is expected to be used most. It allows small to medium source blocks with many repair symbols (k < n <= 255), and 8-bit elements keep memory access byte aligned. For very small blocks, m = 4 (k < n <= 15) is an alternative. For very large blocks, m = 16 (k < n <= 65535) works but has a significant processing cost; lookup tables may need prohibitive memory on embedded platforms, and lighter schemes such as LDPC (RFC 5170) may be preferable.

The use case SHOULD say which values of m must be supported. If it does not, m = 8 MUST be used, and every compliant implementation MUST support at least m = 8.
sections.plainLanguage: Bigger piles can be protected with a heavier method, but that is slow on small gadgets. Most of the time the middle size works well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document defers to the analysis in RFC 6363 and covers only what is specific to Reed-Solomon. If confidentiality matters, one of the RFC 6363 solutions is RECOMMENDED, and so is one for protecting both source and repair packets against corruption. IPsec/ESP is the mandatory-to-implement but not mandatory-to-use baseline.

The FFCI parameters can be attacked: changing the Encoding ID makes the receiver use another scheme, a wrong E or m can cause denial of service, and flipping S can mislead a receiver when symbol size varies between blocks. A larger m also adds decoding load. Tampering with the SBN, ESI or k can corrupt a block. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS integrity protection for the FFCI and for FEC source and repair packets.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster changes the instructions or the labels on the envelopes, the receiver gets confused and cannot rebuild anything. So the instructions and labels should be protected.
